title: Rules
description: How to control Claude Code's behavior with always-on rules and path-conditional rules.

articles.title: What are rules?
articles.summary: Rules are permanent instructions that Claude loads automatically in every session. They have two independent axes: where they live (level) and when they activate (type).

blocks.content:
A rule is a `.md` file that Claude loads automatically — without you having to ask. Every rule has two independent characteristics:

- **Level** — where the file lives: in the project (`.claude/rules/`) or on your system (`~/.claude/rules/`)
- **Type** — when it activates: always (no frontmatter) or only when touching certain files (with `paths:`)

blocks.title: Axis 1 — Level: where does the rule live?

left.label: Project level · .claude/rules/
items: Supports rules with and without paths:

right.label: System level · ~/.claude/rules/
items: Only rules without frontmatter work here

blocks.title: Axis 2 — Type: when does it activate?

left.label: No frontmatter → always active
items: Loads at the start of every session
High attention: at the start of context
File with nothing special at the top

right.label: With paths: → activates by route
items: Loads only when touching a matching file
Applies only to files matching the glob

blocks.title: Rules vs Skills
blocks.content: **Rules** = permanent instructions that Claude always applies. **Skills** = sets of instructions and best practices that Claude consults automatically when a task matches the domain they cover, not only when explicitly requested.

articles.title: Always-active rules (no frontmatter)
articles.summary: .md files with no frontmatter in .claude/rules/ or ~/.claude/rules/. Claude loads them at the start of every session and keeps them in context for the whole conversation.

blocks.content: A `.md` file with no frontmatter in `.claude/rules/` is a rule that loads **always**, at the start of every session. It sits at the beginning of context and stays there even in very long sessions (turn 50+). It's the simplest type and the one with the highest attention weight.

blocks.label: .claude/rules/code-style.md — no frontmatter
blocks.content:
# Code standards — always applies

## TypeScript
- Always use strict TypeScript (strict: true)
- Prefer `type` over `interface` for objects
- Never use `any`, use `unknown` if the type is unknown

## General style
- 2-space indentation
- Single quotes for strings
- Semicolon at the end of every statement

Works at both levels: `.claude/rules/` (project) and `~/.claude/rules/` (system). At the system level it's the **only variant that works** — there's a reported bug (`#21858`) that causes rules with `paths:` to be silently ignored in `~/.claude/`.

rows: Universal code style: strict TypeScript, quotes, indentation
Architecture constraints that must never be broken (e.g. never call the DB from controllers)
Very long instructions → they saturate context from the start
Cross-cutting security guidelines (secret handling, mandatory validations)
Workflows or procedures → that's a skill, not a rule

articles.title: Path-based rules (with paths:)
articles.summary: Rules that only load when Claude works with files matching a glob pattern. Mechanical activation, no reasoning involved. Only work at project level.

blocks.content: Path-based rules use frontmatter with `paths:` to define which files trigger them. The trigger is **mechanical, not semantic**: Claude doesn't evaluate whether it "needs" the rule. If it opens a file matching the glob, the rule loads. If not, it stays on disk. No reasoning involved.

blocks.label: .claude/rules/api-rules.md — with paths
blocks.content:
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# Rules for API endpoints
- All endpoints must validate input with Zod
- Use the standard error format from `src/api/errors.ts`
- Include OpenAPI comments on every route handler
- Return correct HTTP status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, 500)

blocks.label: .claude/rules/frontend-rules.md — brace expansion in glob
blocks.content:
---
paths:
  - "src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"
  - "components/**/*.{ts,tsx}"
---

# Rules for React components
- Use functional components, never classes
- Name handlers with a `handle` prefix (e.g. `handleSubmit`)
- Extract complex logic into custom hooks

blocks.title: Known bug (2026): paths: doesn't work in ~/.claude/
blocks.content: Rules with `paths:` in `~/.claude/rules/` (system level) are **silently ignored**. Path-based rules only work in `.claude/rules/` at the project level. If you need to verify which rules are active, use `/memory` in the session.

items.title: Per-layer conventions
items.description: API, frontend, tests, docs — each layer with its own conventions without polluting the others.

items.title: Monorepos
items.description: Multiple domains or packages with different styles. Each domain has its own rules.

items.title: File-type-specific rules
items.description: Rules that only make sense in a certain file type (e.g. validations only in endpoints).

rows: Layer-specific conventions: API, frontend, tests, DB
Rules that apply to the whole project with no exceptions → those go without frontmatter
Large projects or monorepos where each domain has its own style
Rules in ~/.claude/rules/ → known bug: paths: doesn't work there
When global rules start accumulating exceptions per file type
Workflows or procedures → that's a skill, not a path-based rule

articles.title: CLAUDE.md: levels, inheritance, and precedence
articles.summary: The three levels of CLAUDE.md (project, directory, user), what's shared and what isn't, and how conflicts between rules at different levels are resolved.

blocks.content: CLAUDE.md isn't a single file: there are three levels, each with a different scope. Confusing the correct level is one of the most common mistakes in teams — and one of the most tested topics in the exam.

rows: Only that directory and its subdirectories
The whole team (when working in that dir)
No — lives on the personal machine

blocks.title: The most common mistake: team rules in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
blocks.content: If you put a team rule (e.g. 'always sign commits with GPG') in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, it only applies on **your** machine. The rest of the team will never see it. Team rules must go in the project's `CLAUDE.md`, committed to the repository.

rows.value: Personal developer preferences: favorite editor, shortcuts, response tone
"Always respond in Spanish" or "I prefer explanations with analogies"
Team conventions, architecture constraints, security rules
Team conventions: code style, commit process, technical constraints
"Use tabs for indentation" or "Never push directly to main"
Anything that must apply uniformly across the team

blocks.content:
**Directory inheritance**: Claude loads the CLAUDE.md files from every directory from the root down to the file it's editing. If you're in `backend/payments/`, Claude loads: CLAUDE.md (root) → backend/CLAUDE.md → backend/payments/CLAUDE.md.

**Precedence**: when there's a conflict between a directory CLAUDE.md and one at a higher level, the more specific one (the one closest to the edited file) takes precedence. If the root says 'use tabs' and backend/ says 'use spaces', 'use spaces' wins in backend/.

blocks.title: CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/ can coexist
blocks.content: They're not mutually exclusive. CLAUDE.md is well suited for general project context (system description, tech stack, global conventions). `.claude/rules/` is better for instructions that need conditional loading by glob. Large projects use both together.

blocks.title: A CLAUDE.md change only takes effect after git pull
blocks.content: CLAUDE.md is read from disk at the start of every session. If you update the file and commit it, teammates who haven't done `git pull` still see the previous version. When a teammate reports that Claude isn't following the new rules, the first thing to check is whether they have the updated version of the file.

articles.title: Custom commands (/command)
articles.summary: How to create, place, and parameterize team and individual custom commands. $ARGUMENTS, @path, and when to use each level.

blocks.content: Custom commands are Markdown files invoked with `/filename`. They're the most direct way to turn passive conventions ("Claude should do X before every PR") into active, repeatable workflows.

rows.value: .claude/commands/review-pr.md in the repo
Committed to git — the whole team has it
Team workflows: /review-pr, /deploy, /changelog, /commit
~/.claude/commands/my-workflow.md in your home
Only on your machine — private
Personal workflows that don't apply to the team

blocks.title: The classic mistake: a command that only works for its author
blocks.content: If a command is in `~/.claude/commands/review-pr.md` instead of `.claude/commands/review-pr.md`, it only exists on the author's machine. When the rest of the team clones the repo, the command doesn't exist. The rule: if a command is for the team, it must live in `.claude/commands/` and be committed.

blocks.label: .claude/commands/review-pr.md — with $ARGUMENTS
blocks.content:
# Pull Request Review

Review PR #$ARGUMENTS following our standards:

1. Verify all tests pass
2. Review edge case coverage
3. Confirm the code follows .claude/rules/ conventions
4. Verify the PR has a description and associated Jira tickets
5. Look for obvious security vulnerabilities

Return a summary with: ✅ approved / ⚠️ notes / 🔴 blocking

blocks.title: $ARGUMENTS: the text the user types after the command
blocks.content: When invoking `/review-pr 482`, the string `482` replaces `$ARGUMENTS`. This enables parameterized commands with no extra code. For multiple positional arguments, you can use `$0`, `$1`, `$2`, etc. (0-indexed).

blocks.label: .claude/commands/deploy.md — with @path to share logic
blocks.content:
# Deploy to staging

@.claude/fragments/pre-checks.md

Once checks pass, run the deploy to $ARGUMENTS (environment):

```bash
npm run deploy -- --env=$ARGUMENTS
```

Notify on Slack with the result.

blocks.title: @path: composition without duplication
blocks.content: `@path/to/file.md` loads that file's content inside the command. It lets you extract reusable fragments (pre-checks, formatting templates, checklists) that multiple commands share. If the referenced file doesn't exist, the command fails to parse.

blocks.title: Imports in CLAUDE.md: the same syntax, a different context
blocks.content: The same `@path/to/file.md` mechanism is used inside a CLAUDE.md to import external files and keep it modular — for example, importing only the standards file relevant to each package in a monorepo, instead of a single monolithic CLAUDE.md with every package's conventions. The official docs title this section "Import additional files," but the syntax itself never includes the word "import" — it's the same `@path` as in custom commands, not a special `@import` token.

articles.title: Plan Mode and headless CI
articles.summary: When to use Plan Mode vs. direct execution, and the three essential flags for integrating Claude Code into CI pipelines: -p, --output-format json, and --max-turns.

blocks.content: Plan Mode and headless mode are two ways of adapting Claude Code to different contexts: one for making decisions before acting, the other for running without human intervention.

rows.value: Claude reasons, designs a strategy, and presents the plan — without executing any action yet
Large changes (multiple files), architectural refactors, or when the developer isn't sure of the right approach
Simple, well-scoped tasks — it adds latency and tokens with no real benefit
Shift+Tab in the CLI (toggle), or explicitly instruct Claude to present the plan first
Claude acts immediately: edits files, runs commands, iterates until done
Contained, well-defined tasks: fixing a bug in one file, renaming a function, adding a test
High-risk changes spanning many files, or where the approach isn't clear
It's the default mode — Plan Mode is the exception, not the rule

blocks.content: **Headless CI** — To integrate Claude Code into automated pipelines (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, etc.) there are three flags that form the standard trio:

rows: Non-interactive mode: accepts the prompt as an argument and exits
Claude Code waits for keyboard input — the CI job hangs indefinitely
Structured JSON output instead of plain text
Downstream scripts can't reliably parse the output
Forces the output JSON to conform to a specific schema, not just 'be valid JSON'
The JSON can be syntactically correct but missing fields or shaped in a way the downstream script doesn't expect
Hard limit on agentic loop iterations
The loop can iterate indefinitely on a persistent error — CI job timeout

blocks.label: CI integration — standard invocation
blocks.content:
# The minimal trio for CI:
claude -p "Review the files changed in this PR and report quality issues" \
  --output-format json \
  --max-turns 20

# With CLAUDE.md available to maintain team conventions:
# (The repo's CLAUDE.md loads automatically if it's in the working directory)

blocks.title: -p is the most forgotten flag — and the one that blocks everything
blocks.content: The most common mistake in CI integrations is omitting `-p`. Without it, Claude Code runs in interactive mode and the job waits for keyboard input until it times out. If a Claude Code CI job hangs with no visible errors, the first thing to check is whether `-p` is in the command.

blocks.title: Granular permissions in CI: allow vs. ask
blocks.content: In CI, read-only commands like `grep`, `cat`, or `git diff` should be configured as `allow` (no confirmation) so the job flows. Critical write operations like `git commit` or `git push` should be configured as `ask`, requiring human approval — especially for merges to main, which should never be fully automated.

articles.title: Iterative refinement: examples, tests, and the interview pattern
articles.summary: Three techniques to progressively improve output when a prose instruction isn't enough: concrete input/output examples, test-driven iteration, and the interview pattern where Claude asks before implementing.

blocks.content: When a prose description of what's needed produces inconsistent results across attempts, the problem is almost never that Claude "didn't understand" — it's that the instruction admits more than one valid interpretation. Three techniques converge on resolving that ambiguity in different ways.

items.title: 📋 Concrete input/output examples
items.body: Showing 2-3 input/expected-output pairs is more effective than describing the transformation in words. It removes interpretation ambiguity: instead of "normalize the dates," showing "'15/03/2025' → '2025-03-15'" leaves only one possible behavior.

items.title: 🧪 Test-driven iteration
items.body: Write the test suite first (expected cases, edge cases, performance requirements), then iterate by sharing concrete failures with Claude. Each test failure is a precise instruction of what to fix — much more specific than "it doesn't work right."

items.title: 🎤 Interview pattern
items.body: Before implementing something in a domain with non-obvious decisions (cache invalidation strategy, failure modes, business edge cases), ask Claude to first ask questions instead of assuming. It surfaces design considerations the developer hadn't anticipated, before a single line of code is written.

blocks.label: Interview pattern — how to invoke it
blocks.content:
Before implementing the caching system for the product catalog,
ask me the questions you need about invalidation, TTL, consistency
across replicas, and failure behavior — don't assume anything yet.

# Claude responds with questions like:
# - What happens if two requests update the same product simultaneously?
# - Should the cache invalidate immediately, or is a TTL of a few minutes acceptable?
# - What behavior is expected if the cache service doesn't respond: fall back to the DB or error?
#
# Only after those answers does Claude have the context to design it well.

blocks.title: When to group issues and when to resolve them one by one
blocks.content: If several detected issues interact with each other (fixing one potentially breaks another), it's better to describe them all together in a single message so Claude resolves them in a coordinated way. If they're independent of each other, iterating one at a time lets you verify each fix before continuing, avoiding a large change that's hard to review or revert.

articles.title: Rules, Skills, and CLAUDE.md: when to use each
articles.summary: Quick reference table for deciding which mechanism to use based on the type of instruction.

blocks.content: The three mechanisms cover different use cases. Choosing the right one determines when instructions apply and with what attention weight.

blocks.title: Rules vs CLAUDE.md
blocks.content: CLAUDE.md is the traditional instructions file — it's still valid. The `.claude/rules/` folder is the structured way to organize those same instructions as the project grows. You can use them together: CLAUDE.md for general project context and `.claude/rules/` for segmented instructions.

blocks.title: Position in context matters
blocks.content: Rules (with or without frontmatter) enter **at the start of context** when activated — they get high attention throughout the session. Skills enter mid-conversation and can lose attention in long sessions. For critical instructions that must never be forgotten, use rules, not skills.
